pos: n. (Conrad Pellican, 1478–1556, Hebraist of Zurich and the first German to print a Hebrew grammar)
etymology: German Konrad, bold counsel; Pellican, a latinised form of the surname Kursner, a furrier.
biblical_def: Conrad Pellican taught himself Hebrew out of a borrowed manuscript, with no grammar, no dictionary, and no teacher, by comparing the Hebrew text of a psalm with a Latin version until the letters gave up their values. In 1504, at twenty-six, he printed the result: the first Hebrew grammar published by a Christian in Germany, four years before Reuchlin's. He was then a Franciscan; he left the order in 1526 and spent his last thirty years at Zurich as professor of Hebrew and Greek under Zwingli and Bullinger, producing a commentary on the whole Bible and sharing in the Zurich Latin Bible. The self-taught beginning is the point worth keeping. A man with a borrowed manuscript and no apparatus worked out a language because he had decided that the Old Testament should be read in the words God gave it, and that nothing less was reading it. Everything the Reformation did with the Hebrew text stands on work of that kind, done by men who had to make the tools first. “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety, and rudiments as the first principles of any art or science.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
RU'DIMENT, n. A first principle or element; the first rules or principles of any art or science.
FRI'AR, n. A brother of a religious order; an appellation common to the monks of all orders.
CONJUGA'TION, n. In grammar, the distribution of the several inflections or variations of a verb.

If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures;
Pro 2:5

Pro 2:3
Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding;
Rom 3:2

corruption_summary: The self-taught Franciscan who printed the first Christian Hebrew grammar in Germany.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the original languages are an advanced study, taken up after the real work of theology is under way. Pellican had the order exactly reversed and so did his whole generation. The grammar came first, because until the text can be read there is no theology to do; and he made the grammar before he had the standing, the leisure or the materials for it.

The principle to recover is that Scripture describes the pursuit of the knowledge of God as mining, with all the labour the figure implies. “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4). Nobody digs silver by accident. And the promise is attached to the digging, not to the wish: “Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God” (Pro 2:5). The oracles were committed in Hebrew and Greek (Rom 3:2), and somebody in every generation has to be able to read them.

pos: n. (Sebastian Münster, 1488–1552, Hebraist and cosmographer of Basel)
etymology: Greek Sebastianos, venerable, august; German Münster, a minster, from Latin monasterium.
biblical_def: Sebastian Münster learned his Hebrew from Pellican, left the Franciscans, and settled at Basel, where he gave the Protestant world its working Old Testament. His Hebrew Bible of 1534–35 printed the Hebrew text with a fresh Latin translation beside it and his own notes drawn from the Jewish commentators beneath — the first time a Christian scholar had made the rabbinic exposition generally available to Latin readers who could then judge it for themselves. He published Hebrew and Aramaic grammars and dictionaries, a Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, and later the Cosmographia, the great descriptive geography of the age. His work has limits: the Latin is wooden where the Hebrew is difficult, and he follows his Jewish authorities further than a Christian reading of the Old Testament should. What he did was put the text and its oldest expositors on the same page and trust the reader. “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cosmography as the description of the world or universe, and rabbinical as pertaining to the rabbins or their opinions and learning.
webster_full: COSMOG'RAPHY, n. The science of the general system or constitution of the world; a description of the world.
RABBIN'ICAL, a. Pertaining to the rabbins, or to their opinions, learning and language.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
AN'NOTATION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;
corruption_summary: The Basel Hebrew Bible that printed the text, a fresh Latin version, and the Jewish commentators together.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is a real one in Münster's own method rather than a modern distortion. He leaned heavily on the medieval Jewish expositors, and where those commentators turn a messianic text away from Christ he too often follows them. The Jewish grammarians are indispensable on the language and are not a safe guide to the sense of the prophets, and the two services have to be kept apart.

The principle to recover is the Lord's own rule of Old Testament interpretation, given on the Emmaus road and binding on every Hebraist since: “And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). That is the controlling sense. Paul meanwhile grants Israel everything that is honestly theirs, and it is a great deal: “to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law” (Rom 9:4).

pos: n. (Elias Levita, 1469–1549, Jewish grammarian and teacher of the Christian Hebraists)
etymology: Hebrew Eliyahu, the LORD is God; Levita, the Levite, from the tribe of Levi.
biblical_def: Elias Levita was a Jewish grammarian of Germany and Italy who did more than any other single man to put Hebrew into Christian hands. He taught the language to Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo in Rome for thirteen years, and afterwards worked at the press of Paul Fagius at Isny, where his grammars, his concordance and his lexicons were printed for a Christian readership. He was criticised by other Jews for teaching the Torah's language to Gentiles and answered that the knowledge was not his to withhold. His most consequential book is the Massoreth ha-Massoreth of 1538, in which he argued from the evidence that the vowel points of the Hebrew Bible were added by the Masoretes after the Talmud, not given at Sinai. The argument split Christian scholarship for the next two centuries and still divides it. Whatever is finally concluded about the points, Levita's method was the honest one: he set out the evidence and let it tell. “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Pro 30:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines masoretic as relating to the Masora, the Jewish criticism of the Hebrew text, and vowel-point as a mark placed under a consonant to indicate a vowel.
webster_full: MASORET'IC, a. Relating to the Masora, or to the notes and criticisms of the Hebrew text made by the Jewish doctors.
POINT, n. In grammar, a mark used to distinguish sentences or parts; in Hebrew, a mark denoting a vowel.
GRAMMA'RIAN, n. One versed in grammar, or the construction of languages; a philologist.
CONCORD'ANCE, n. A dictionary in which the principal words used in the scriptures are arranged alphabetically.
scriptures: Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Mat 5:18

Rom 3:2

corruption_summary: The Jewish grammarian who taught the Christian Hebraists and dated the vowel points.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse of Levita's finding is to treat a question about the pointing as a question about the text. The vowel points are a system of marks indicating pronunciation, added to a consonantal text that the Jewish scribes had transmitted with extraordinary care for centuries before them. Whether the marks are late is a historical question about an editorial apparatus. Whether the words are God's is a different question entirely, and nothing in Levita touches it.

The principle to recover is that the preservation Scripture claims for itself is claimed at the level of the smallest written element and is claimed by the Lord himself. “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). The purity of the words is likewise asserted as a thing tested rather than assumed: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6).

pos: n. (Paul Fagius, 1504–1549, Hebraist of Isny and Strasbourg, professor at Cambridge)
etymology: Latin Paulus, little, small; Fagius, a latinised form of Buchlein, a little beech tree.
biblical_def: Paul Fagius was pastor at Isny in Swabia when he set up a Hebrew press there and brought Elias Levita to run it, and between them in three years they printed the grammars, lexicons and concordance that equipped a generation of Christian Hebraists. He went on to Strasbourg, then to Heidelberg, and in 1549 Archbishop Cranmer brought him and Martin Bucer to England, Fagius to be reader in Hebrew at Cambridge. He died of fever within months of arriving, before he had delivered a lecture. In 1557, under Mary, the bodies of Fagius and Bucer were dug up, chained to stakes in Cambridge market place, and burned with their books; under Elizabeth the university held a formal ceremony restoring their degrees. The episode is grotesque and it is also clarifying. A regime that exhumes a dead Hebrew professor to burn him is confessing that the thing it fears is not the man but what he put into print. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exhume as to dig out of the earth what has been buried, and posthumous as done or published after one's death.
webster_full: EXHU'ME, v. To dig out of the earth what has been buried; to disinter.
POST'HUMOUS, a. Born after the death of the father, or taken from the dead body of the mother; published after the death of the author.
READ'ER, n. One who reads; an officer in a university who reads lectures on a science.
IGNOM'INY, n. Public disgrace; shame; reproach; dishonour.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: The Isny Hebrew press, Cambridge, and a body burned in the market place eight years dead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern embarrassment that treats the Marian exhumations as a curiosity of a cruder age, a story about bad manners rather than about doctrine. It was a deliberate act with a stated purpose: the books were burned with the bones, and the sentence was pronounced against the men's writings as heresy. The object was to destroy what they had taught.

The principle to recover is that the word outlasts every apparatus brought against it, and Scripture states this in exactly the form the Cambridge bonfire tested. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter repeats it and then adds the application that makes it personal: “And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you” (1Pe 1:25). The thing they could not burn was already in other men's hands.

pos: n. (Sanctes Pagninus, 1470–1536, Dominican Hebraist and Latin translator of the whole Bible)
etymology: Latin sanctus, holy; Pagninus, from paganus, of the country district, a surname of Lucca.
biblical_def: Sanctes Pagninus was a Dominican of Lucca who produced in 1528 the first complete Latin translation of the whole Bible made afresh from the Hebrew and Greek since Jerome. He worked at it for about twenty-five years. His Latin is often harsh, because he rendered the Hebrew so closely that the word order shows through, and that very woodenness made it the standard study text for a century: a man who wanted to know what the Hebrew said, rather than what good Latin would say, reached for Pagninus. Servetus and others later issued editions; the Protestant Hebraists used him constantly. He also carried through the Old Testament the division into numbered verses that had been developing in Jewish and Christian practice, and his influence on the numbering we use is direct. He remained in his own communion and we do not pretend otherwise; the system he died in holds a tradition beside Scripture and an altar sacrifice we must refuse. His labour on the text is real and the Reformers used it without embarrassment. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines literal as according to the letter, following the exact words, and verse as a short division of any composition, particularly of the Scriptures.
webster_full: LIT'ERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; following the letter or exact words.
VERSE, n. A short division of any composition; particularly, a division of the chapters of the Bible.
DOMIN'ICAN, n. One of an order of friars founded by Dominic de Guzman.
IDI'OM, n. A mode of expression peculiar to a language; a peculiarity of expression.

Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: The Dominican whose wooden Latin from the Hebrew became the Protestant study Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two live misuses meet here. One is the reflex that a scholar's communion settles the value of his philology, so that a Dominican's collation of Hebrew manuscripts may be ignored. The Reformers did not reason that way and were right not to: a true reading is true whoever establishes it. The other is the opposite error of letting honest admiration for a man's learning soften the judgment on the system he served, which holds tradition beside Scripture and repeats a sacrifice Christ finished.

The principle to recover is that God committed the oracles to a custody and then required the sense to be given. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2) is about the deposit; “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) is about the duty laid on whoever handles it. Pagninus served the second well. He is used, not followed: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).

pos: n. (Johannes Drusius, 1550–1616, orientalist of Oxford, Leiden and Franeker)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Drusius, a latinised form of the Flemish surname Van den Driessche.
biblical_def: Johannes Drusius was a Fleming whose father fled the Spanish persecution, which is how a boy from Oudenaarde came to learn his Hebrew in England and lecture on it at Oxford at twenty-two. He taught afterwards at Leiden and then for thirty years at Franeker in Friesland. His speciality was the illumination of the New Testament from Jewish sources — the customs, the idioms, the sayings and the sects that the Gospels assume and do not explain — and he published a long series of philological commentaries that later scholars quarried without always naming him. The States-General commissioned him to annotate the difficult places of the Old Testament, a task he worked at for years. He was criticised, as Münster had been, for leaning on rabbinic authorities, and the criticism is only partly fair: knowing what a first-century Jew meant by a phrase is not the same as accepting a rabbi's doctrine. “And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines orientalist as one versed in the eastern languages, and philology as the study of language, grammar and criticism.
webster_full: O'RIENTALIST, n. An inhabitant of an eastern country; one versed in the eastern languages and literature.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language; grammatical learning; criticism.
ID'IOM, n. A mode of expression peculiar to a language.
AN'NOTATE, v. To comment; to make remarks on a writing.

corruption_summary: The Franeker orientalist who lit the New Testament from the customs it assumes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the handling of background study as though it were the key to Scripture, so that a passage means whatever the reconstructed context permits and the plain sense is held hostage to the latest view of first-century custom. Drusius did not work that way; he supplied the usage and left the doctrine to the text. But the method he helped found has often been turned into a solvent.

The principle to recover is that understanding of Scripture is finally a gift and not merely an achievement of learning. The disciples on the road had the Scriptures and a perfect Expositor beside them, and Luke still records a second act: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45). Philology serves that opening and cannot substitute for it. What learning can do is remove avoidable obstacles, which is honest work.

pos: n. (Johann Buxtorf the elder, 1564–1629, professor of Hebrew at Basel)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Buxtorf, from a Westphalian place-name, box-tree village.
biblical_def: Johann Buxtorf held the Hebrew chair at Basel for thirty-eight years and was called in his own lifetime the master of the rabbis. He produced the grammar, the lexicon, the concordance and the great Rabbinic Bible of 1618–19 that Protestant students used for two centuries, and he knew the Jewish literature better than almost any Christian before him. He is also the chief defender of the position Elias Levita had attacked: that the Hebrew vowel points are ancient and authoritative, not a late Masoretic addition. His son carried the argument on against Louis Cappel, and the Helvetic Consensus of 1675 wrote the Buxtorf position into a confession. Later scholarship has not sustained it. The honest account is that Buxtorf and his son were defending something true — the integrity and authority of the received Hebrew text — by means of a historical claim about the pointing that the evidence will not carry, and that the true thing does not depend on the claim. “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lexicographer as the author of a dictionary, and integrity as entireness, unbroken state, soundness.
webster_full: LEXICOG'RAPHER, n. The author of a lexicon or dictionary.
INTEG'RITY, n. Wholeness; entireness; unbroken state; the entire, unimpaired state of anything.
MAS'ORA, n. A Hebrew work on the Bible by several rabbins, containing a critical collection of remarks on the text.
AUTHEN'TIC, a. Having a genuine original or authority; of approved authority.

corruption_summary: The master of the rabbis, and a true doctrine defended by a historical claim that failed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the use of the Buxtorf–Cappel quarrel as a demonstration that confessional scholarship is driven by dogma rather than evidence, and therefore that nothing it concluded can be trusted. The episode shows something narrower and more instructive. Buxtorf tied a doctrine he was right about to an auxiliary historical claim he was wrong about, and when the claim fell his opponents took the doctrine with it in the public mind, though it never depended on the claim at all.

The principle to recover is that the preservation of Scripture is asserted by Scripture concerning the words and the letters, and does not rest on any theory about an editorial apparatus. “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35) is the Lord's own form of the claim, and he hangs an argument on a single word in the verse he is quoting. “The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) says the same of the whole. Defend what Scripture claims, and no more, and the defence will hold.

pos: n. (Jean Mercier, d. 1570, royal professor of Hebrew in Paris)
etymology: French Jean, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Mercier, a mercer, a dealer in cloth.
biblical_def: Jean Mercier succeeded François Vatable in the royal Hebrew chair in Paris in 1546 and held it for a quarter of a century, the most accomplished Christian Hebraist France produced in that century. He commented on Genesis, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the minor prophets, edited Chaldee paraphrases, and wrote on Hebrew grammar; Beza and the Genevans regarded him highly and he appears to have held Reformed convictions privately while keeping a royal appointment in a kingdom that was burning Protestants. He left Paris in 1570 and died of plague at Uzès, which spared him the Saint Bartholomew's massacre by two years. The quiet of his career is itself a datum about France: the most learned Hebraist in the kingdom could not say openly what he believed, and the learning went on in a chair under a crown that would shortly murder his brethren in the street. Open suffering is one form of the cost and a silent chair is another, and the apostle will allow neither as a substitute for confession: “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines professor as one that publicly teaches any science, and Chaldee as the language of the Chaldeans, the Aramaic of the Old Testament.
webster_full: PROFES'SOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; an officer in a university.

corruption_summary: The royal Hebraist of Paris, learned in a kingdom where he could not say what he believed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romance of the private believer, the man who holds the truth inwardly in a hostile place and whose silence is counted as prudence or even as a subtler kind of witness. Mercier's scholarship is genuinely valuable and his position was genuinely dangerous, and neither fact turns silence into confession.

The principle to recover is that the confession is public by definition and that Scripture never treats this as negotiable. “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) is a word about profession, which is a thing said out loud. Paul states the matter as an absence of shame: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” (Rom 1:16). And the calculation that makes open confession rational is given by the Lord: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28).

pos: n. (the Antwerp Polyglot, 1568–1573, the Biblia Regia printed by Christopher Plantin)
etymology: Dutch Antwerpen, a city of Brabant; Greek polyglottos, many-tongued, from polys, many, and glossa, a tongue.
biblical_def: The Antwerp Polyglot, called the Royal Bible because Philip II paid for it, is eight folio volumes printed by Christopher Plantin between 1568 and 1573 under the editorship of Benito Arias Montano. It sets out the Hebrew, the Greek, the Vulgate, the Septuagint in Latin, the Aramaic Targums with Latin versions, and for the New Testament the Syriac, with grammars and dictionaries of the biblical languages filling the last volumes. It is the largest scholarly undertaking of the sixteenth century and it was done in a city then being torn apart by the Dutch revolt. Its politics were tangled: Montano was accused at Rome of favouring the Hebrew text above the Vulgate and had to defend himself, and Protestant scholars used the volumes freely while the crown that financed them was executing Protestants in the same provinces. That is the recurring shape of the century. The apparatus of biblical scholarship was built across the confessional line by men who would not have shared a table. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines polyglot as having or containing many languages, and folio as a book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.

corruption_summary: Eight folio volumes of the biblical languages, printed under a crown then executing Protestants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a simple failure of historical honesty in both directions. Protestant accounts have sometimes written the Antwerp volumes out of the story because of who paid for them; Roman accounts have sometimes presented Montano's labours as a vindication of the Vulgate, which the volumes themselves refute by setting the Hebrew beside it and letting a reader compare.

The principle to recover is that God's intention from Pentecost forward has been a word carried in every tongue, and a polyglot is that intention in print. At Pentecost the astonishment was linguistic: “every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6), and what they heard was not a translation of a message but “the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) in their own speech. The end of it is sung in Revelation, where the redeemed are gathered “out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9).

pos: n. (the London Polyglot, 1654–1657, Brian Walton's Biblia Sacra Polyglotta)
etymology: English London, the capital city; Greek polyglottos, many-tongued.
biblical_def: The London Polyglot is the last and greatest of the great polyglot Bibles: six folio volumes edited by Brian Walton and published between 1654 and 1657, with Edmund Castell's heptaglot lexicon following in two more. It prints the Hebrew, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, the Vulgate, the Targums, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Ethiopic and the Persian as the texts allow, each with a Latin version, together with prolegomena on the history and transmission of the text that amount to the first serious critical introduction in English scholarship. It was funded by public subscription rather than a crown — one of the earliest books so financed — and it was produced in England during the Protectorate by a man who was an episcopalian royalist and afterwards a bishop. Walton's prolegomena, in discussing variant readings openly, drew fire from John Owen, who feared the effect on confidence in the text. Owen's concern was serious and Walton's answer was the right one: the variants exist whether they are printed or not. “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prolegomena as preliminary observations or introductory remarks to a book, and various reading as a difference in the text among manuscripts.
webster_full: PROLEGOM'ENA, n. Preliminary observations to a book; introductory remarks prefixed to a work.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. A sum subscribed, or the paper on which names are subscribed for the support of an undertaking.
VA'RIOUS, a. Different; several; manifold; as the various readings of a text.
HEPT'AGLOT, n. A book in seven languages.

corruption_summary: Six folios in nine languages, funded by subscription, and the quarrel with John Owen over variants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse comes from two opposite quarters and both were present in 1657. One says that printing the variants destroys the doctrine of preservation, which was substantially Owen's fear; the other says the variants destroy the doctrine in fact, which is the sceptical use made of the same data ever since. Both assume that preservation means a text transmitted without any variation in any copy, which is not what Scripture claims and not what anyone has ever observed.

The principle to recover is that the word is kept by God through ordinary means, including the labour of comparing copies, and that the claim it makes for itself survives that comparison. “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). The purity asserted is purity under testing: “as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6). And the Bereans are commended precisely for checking: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
